title: Effect of intercritical annealing temperature on microstructure and mechanical properties of a V–Mo alloyed medium–Mn steel
abstract: Medium-Mn steels have attracted considerable attention due to their excellent synergy of high strength and good ductility, making them promising candidates for automotive lightweighting applications. In this study, the effects of intercritical annealing temperature on microstructure, reverted austenite formation, precipitation behavior, and mechanical properties of a V–Mo alloyed medium-Mn steel were systematically investigated. Multi-scale characterization and mechanical testing were employed, and strengthening mechanisms were quantitatively analyzed. Results show that increasing the annealing temperature from 600 °C to 650 °C significantly promotes reverted austenite formation, while simultaneously decreasing its stability due to reduced Mn and C enrichment. Accordingly, increasing the annealing temperature promotes a more pronounced TRIP effect, which contributes to the improved ductility of the steel. Strengthening mechanism calculations indicate that strength degradation originates mainly from reduced dislocation strengthening, together with increased soft-phase reverted austenite at higher temperatures. Consequently, yield strength, tensile strength, and impact toughness continuously decrease, while elongation improves. The steel annealed at 600 °C exhibits the best strength-toughness synergy, achieving 1193 MPa yield strength, 1251 MPa tensile strength, and 78 J impact energy at 0 °C.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: With the rapid development of the automotive industry, increasing the strength of structural steels contributes to vehicle lightweighting, which enhances fuel economy and reduces greenhouse gas emissions while simultaneously improving crashworthiness performance during collisions [ 1–3 ]. Advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) have been widely adopted in automotive manufacturing because of their desirable strength-ductility synergy [ 4–6 ]. The development of AHSS has progressed to the third generation, including quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels and TRIP-aided bainite ferrite (TBF) steels, whose strength-ductility products generally reach 20-40 GPa·% [ 7–9 ]. Compared with other AHSS, medium-Mn steels are particularly attractive due to their simpler processing routes and more balanced mechanical performance.

Typical medium-Mn steels consist of martensite, ferrite, and metastable austenite. During plastic deformation, the retained/reverted austenite transforms to martensite, enabling the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, which improves both strength and ductility [ 10–12 ]. Intercritical annealing (IA) within the (α + γ) two-phase region is the most effective method to form reverted austenite in medium-Mn steels. The resulting reverted austenite content, morphology, and stability are highly sensitive to the IA temperature through element diffusion and partitioning mechanisms [ 12–14 ]. In general, lower IA temperatures promote higher enrichment of C and Mn in austenite, leading to improved austenite stability, whereas higher temperatures facilitate austenite growth but reduce its chemical stability [ 15–17 ].

Despite the outstanding mechanical strength and ductility, medium-Mn steels often exhibit inferior low-temperature toughness, primarily due to the instability of reverted austenite and grain-boundary segregation of Mn, which increases the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature [ 18–20 ]. To address these challenges, microalloying elements such as V and Mo can be added to enhance precipitation strengthening and improve microstructural refinement, while small additions of Ti facilitate nanoscale TiN formation that inhibits grain growth [ 21–23 ]. Optimizing heat treatment design, especially intercritical annealing temperature, is therefore essential for achieving improved strength-toughness balance.

In this study, a V–Mo alloyed medium-Mn steel was designed, and the influence of three different intercritical annealing temperatures on microstructure, reverted austenite behavior, precipitation characteristics, and mechanical properties was systematically investigated [ 15 , 23 , 24 ]. Strengthening mechanisms were quantitatively evaluated to reveal the underlying structure-property relationships [ 25 ]. The findings provide a theoretical basis and technical references for expanding the industrial application of high-performance medium-Mn steels.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: The experimental steel was smelted in a 50 kg vacuum induction furnace, cast, and forged into block billets with a thickness of 60 mm, followed by air cooling to room temperature. The chemical composition of the steel (wt.%) was 0.17C-0.24Si-5.04Mn-0.4V-0.5Mo-0.017Ti, with Fe as the balance. After homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h, the billets were hot-rolled in five passes into 16 mm-thick plates. The initial rolling temperature was 1100 °C and the final rolling temperature was 900 °C. After rolling, the plates were cooled to 600 °C using a laminar cooling system and held for 2 h to simulate coiling, followed by furnace cooling to room temperature.

Thermo-Calc software was used to calculate the  A

                      , the annealing temperatures were selected within the intercritical (α + γ) region to introduce reverted austenite into the microstructure. Annealing was carried out at 600, 620, and 650 °C for 3 h, followed by air cooling to room temperature. According to GB/T 228-2021 Metallic materials-Tensile testing-Part 1 :  Method of test at room temperature, tensile specimens with a diameter of 12 mm, total length of 65 mm, and gauge length of 30 mm were machined from the annealed plates along the transverse direction using wire electrical discharge machining. Tensile tests were conducted at room temperature on a WE-300 hydraulic testing machine at a strain rate of 1 mm/min. In accordance with GB/T 229-2020 Metallic materials-Charpy pendulum impact test method, V-notch Charpy specimens with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm were machined from the intercritically annealed plates along the rolling direction. Impact tests were performed at 0 °C using a JBN-300 N impact testing machine, and fracture morphologies were examined using an FEI Quanta 650 scanning electron microscope. For each annealing condition, two parallel tensile specimens and three parallel impact specimens were tested, and the reported values represent the averages of the parallel samples.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) specimens with dimensions of 12 × 12 × 7 mm were machined from the plates annealed at different temperatures. After sequential grinding with SiC papers of increasing grit size and subsequent polishing, the samples were etched in 4% nital for 30 s, rinsed with water, and air-dried. The microstructures were examined using an FEI Quanta 650 scanning electron microscope.

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) samples, also sized 12 × 12 × 7 mm, were mechanically ground and polished, followed by electrolytic polishing in a mixed solution of glacial acetic acid and perchloric acid (volume ratio 9:1) at 10 V for 10 s. EBSD measurements were performed on an FEI Quanta 650 SEM. A scan area of 50 μm × 50 μm and a step size of 0.08 μm were selected. The acquired data were processed using HKL Channel 5 software.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) specimens with dimensions of 20 × 20 × 5 mm were ground and polished, and surface stresses were removed by electrolytic etching in an aqueous solution containing 15 g KCl and 3 g monohydrate citric acid at 1.4 V. XRD tests were carried out on a D8 ADVANCE diffractometer using a Co Kα radiation source. The scan step size was 0.02°, and the 2θ range was 45-115°. Thin sheets with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm and a thickness of 300 μm were cut from the plates annealed at different temperatures. After sequential grinding with SiC papers of various grit sizes, the sheets were thinned to approximately 40 μm and then punched into 3 mm discs. These discs were further thinned using a twin-jet electrolytic polisher to prepare transmission electron microscopy (TEM) specimens. The microstructures were finally examined using an FEI TECNAI G2 F20 transmission electron microscope.

sections.heading: Microstructure characterization
paragraphs:
The SEM microstructures of the experimental steel annealed at different temperatures are shown in  Fig. 2 
                         . After intercritical annealing, the room-temperature microstructure consists predominantly of annealed martensite together with a large number of corrosion pits. During intercritical annealing, C and Mn partition from annealed martensite into the reverted austenite [ 27 ]. Local variations in chemical composition weaken the interfacial bonding strength, causing reverted austenite or fresh martensite formed from reverted austenite to detach during etching, thereby generating corrosion pits [ 28 ]. Consequently, the distribution and morphology of corrosion pits can qualitatively reflect the amount and characteristics of reverted austenite [ 11 ]. After annealing at 600 °C, most of the corrosion pits exhibit blocky morphologies ( Fig. 2 (a, b)). At 620 °C, the pits become noticeably larger ( Fig. 2 (c, d)). When the annealing temperature is increased to 650 °C, the number of pits increases and they become more densely distributed; the proportion of thin-film-like pits also rises ( Fig. 2 (e, f)).

Fig. 3 
                          shows the phase distribution maps of the steel annealed at different temperatures. In the maps, the red regions correspond to FCC austenite, whereas the gray regions represent BCC martensite. As shown in  Fig. 3 (a), only a small amount of fine, granular reverted austenite is observed after annealing at 600 °C. When the annealing temperature is increased to 620 °C, the volume fraction of reverted austenite increases significantly ( Fig. 3 (b)); it remains predominantly granular in morphology and is mainly distributed along prior austenite grain boundaries. After annealing at 650 °C, both the volume fraction and size of reverted austenite reach their maximum ( Fig. 3 (c)), and thin-film reverted austenite appears between martensite laths. These observations are consistent with the SEM results in  Fig. 2 .

It is also noted that the reverted austenite is primarily distributed at high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs). This is because the high energy of HAGBs provides a driving force for the nucleation of reverted austenite, and because HAGBs serve as major diffusion pathways, thereby facilitating the austenite reversion process [ 29 ].

Fig. 4 
                          shows the IPF maps of the experimental steel annealed at different temperatures. It can be observed that the grain size decreases significantly with the increase of annealing temperature. The equivalent circular grain sizes of the specimens annealed at different temperatures were statistically analyzed, and the corresponding average grain sizes are shown in  Fig. 4 (d). The grain size of the experimental steel exhibits a decreasing trend as the annealing temperature increases, reaching the minimum value after annealing at 650 °C. Two factors are considered to contribute to the reduction of effective grain size. First, increasing the annealing temperature reduces the stability of the reverted austenite. Some reverted austenite with poor stability transforms into martensite upon destabilization [ 30 ]. The newly formed fresh martensite has different orientations from the original martensite matrix, which results in an overall refinement of martensitic grains. When the size of the fresh martensite is small, it behaves as a new block unit and thus reduces the effective grain size of the steel. Second, a large number of fine granular phases can be observed in  Fig. 4 (b, c), which, by comparison with  Fig. 3 , are identified as reverted austenite. As the annealing temperature increases, the volume fraction of reverted austenite increases significantly, which also contributes to the reduction of effective grain size.

The XRD patterns of the experimental steel annealed at different temperatures are shown in  Fig. 5 
                         (a). Diffraction peaks corresponding to both BCC and FCC phases are present under all heat-treatment conditions. With increasing annealing temperature, the intensity of the austenite diffraction peaks also increases, indicating a higher volume fraction of reverted austenite. As shown in  Fig. 5 (b), the austenite content of the experimental steel exhibits an almost linear increase. After annealing at 600 °C, 620 °C, and 650 °C, the austenite contents are approximately 2%, 10%, and 20%, respectively. The increase in annealing temperature enhances the diffusion coefficient of Mn [ 31 ], accelerating the partitioning of Mn from martensite to reverted austenite, thereby promoting the formation of reverted austenite. However, the higher volume fraction of austenite leads to a decrease in its average Mn concentration, which consequently reduces its stability [ 32 ].

Fig. 6 (b)  presents the TEM microstructures of the experimental steel after annealing at different temperatures. The room-temperature microstructures under different annealing conditions consist of reverted austenite and annealed martensite. As shown in  Fig. 6 (a), the reverted austenite obtained after annealing at 600 °C exhibits both granular and thin-film morphologies. EDS line scanning was carried out along the region marked in  Fig. 6 (a), traversing the martensitic matrix and reverted austenite successively. The results, shown in  Fig. 6 (b), reveal significant fluctuations in Mn content along the scanned line. By correlating with  Fig. 6 (a), the regions with higher Mn concentration correspond to reverted austenite. This confirms that the thin-film austenite within the scanned area is the reverted austenite formed during annealing, and that pronounced Mn partitioning occurs between the annealed martensite and the reverted austenite.

When the annealing temperature increases to 620 °C, both the film-like and granular reverted austenite phases exhibit a noticeable increase in size ( Fig. 6 (c–f)), indicating that the higher annealing temperature promotes the growth of reverted austenite [ 12 ]. When the annealing temperature was further increased to 650 °C, the reverted austenite becomes even longer and wider, and both granular and thin-film morphologies gradually evolve into larger blocky or lath-like structures ( Fig. 6 (g and h)). From the bright-field images at different temperatures, it can be observed that the film- or lath-like retained austenite always exists between martensite laths.

Selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) was performed at the interface between a martensite lath and an austenite lath shown in  Fig. 6 (h). After indexing the diffraction spots, it was found that a Kurdjumov-Sachs (K–S) orientation relationship exists between the austenite lath and the adjacent martensite laths ( Fig. 6 (i)), confirming that lath- or thin-film reverted austenite nucleates preferentially between martensite laths.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic and kinetic calculation
paragraphs:
The phase fractions of FCC and BCC phases, as well as the C and Mn contents in austenite, were simulated using Thermo-Calc software, as shown in  Fig. 7 
                         . With increasing temperature, the mass fraction of martensite gradually decreases, while the mass fraction of austenite increases until a fully austenitic single-phase structure is obtained ( Fig. 7 (a)). The C and Mn contents in austenite continuously decrease with the rise in temperature ( Fig. 7 (b)), indicating that the average concentrations of C and Mn in austenite gradually decrease during intercritical annealing. Since C and Mn are strong austenite-stabilizing elements, the chemical stability of reverted austenite decreases as the intercritical annealing temperature increases [ 33 ].

Since the density of prior-austenite grain boundaries is considerably lower than that of martensite lath boundaries, reverted austenite preferentially nucleates at martensite lath boundaries [ 11 ]. The subsequent growth of reverted austenite proceeds through the migration of the newly formed γ/α interface. The γ/α interfaces revealed by TEM ( Fig. 6 ) are approximately planar and exhibit low curvature, but remain capable of migration. For an approximately planar interface, the curvature-driven capillary force is negligible because normal interface migration causes little change in the total interfacial area. Nevertheless, the interface can migrate in the direction normal to itself under the driving forces arising from the bulk chemical free-energy difference between the γ and α phases and the chemical-potential gradients of the alloying elements across the interface [ 34 ]. During intercritical annealing at 600-650 °C, the formation of reverted austenite and the redistribution of C and Mn reduce the total chemical free energy of the system. In addition, the high dislocation density and lattice distortion stored in the quenched martensitic matrix may provide an additional contribution to the transformation driving force.

The TEM-EDS line scan in  Fig. 6  reveals Mn enrichment in the film-like reverted austenite of the specimen annealed at 600 °C, qualitatively confirming the partitioning of Mn from tempered martensite into reverted austenite during intercritical annealing. However, this result is not intended to quantitatively determine the C and Mn contents in austenite or to compare their evolution at different annealing temperatures. The equilibrium austenite fraction and the average C and Mn contents in austenite were therefore evaluated using Thermo-Calc, as shown in  Fig. 7 , whereas the local redistribution of C and Mn and the migration behavior of the γ/α interface were further investigated using DICTRA.

Considering the high density of martensite lath boundaries in the quenched steel, a one-dimensional DICTRA model was established to simulate γ/α interface migration and the C and Mn concentration profiles on both sides of the interface. The initial widths of the γ and α regions were set to 2 and 100 nm, respectively, and the calculation was performed using a half-width model. The simulation results are presented in  Fig. 8 
                         . With increasing annealing temperature, the calculated austenite width increases, whereas the width of the martensitic region decreases, indicating that the γ/α interface progressively migrates into the tempered martensite matrix. The greater migration distance at higher temperatures is associated with the enhanced diffusivities of C and Mn and the increased equilibrium austenite fraction.

At the initial stage of austenite reversion, a pronounced C-enrichment peak appears on the austenite side of the γ/α interface, whereas the Mn content remains close to the nominal composition of the steel. This result suggests that early-stage interface migration is primarily promoted by the rapid interstitial diffusion of C and is consistent with the negligible-partition local-equilibrium (NPLE) mode proposed by Nakada et al. [ 35 ]. As austenite growth proceeds, C is rapidly redistributed, and its concentration profile gradually approaches equilibrium. In contrast, because of the substantially lower substitutional diffusivity of Mn, a pronounced Mn concentration gradient remains near the γ/α interface, even at 650 °C. Consequently, the later stage of interface migration becomes increasingly dependent on Mn partitioning, corresponding to the partition local-equilibrium (PLE) mode [ 36 ].

The Thermo-Calc and DICTRA calculations predict that increasing the intercritical annealing temperature increases the equilibrium fraction and width of reverted austenite while decreasing its average enrichment in C and Mn. The reduced solute enrichment suggests a decrease in the chemical stability of reverted austenite at higher annealing temperatures [ 37–39 ]. Moreover, the simulated concentration gradients within the austenite indicate spatial variations in chemical stability, with regions containing lower local C and Mn contents being less chemically stabilized. In addition, the XRD, EBSD, and TEM results demonstrate that both the volume fraction and size of reverted austenite increase with increasing annealing temperature. These experimental observations are consistent with the simulated increase in austenite formation and the predicted reduction in average C and Mn enrichment.

sections.heading: Precipitate characterization
paragraphs:
Fig. 9 
                          presents the TEM characterization of the precipitates in the experimental steel after intercritical annealing at 600 °C, 620 °C, and 650 °C. As shown in  Fig. 9 (a-c), two distinct populations of precipitates are observed under all annealing conditions: fine short rod-like or needle-like precipitates and relatively coarse ellipsoidal or disc-like precipitates. EDS point analyses were performed to characterize the fine precipitates in the specimens annealed at different temperatures. The elemental compositions indicate that these fine precipitates are V- and Mo-rich MC-type carbides. The intercritical annealing temperature has a pronounced effect on the relative contents of V and Mo in the VC precipitates. At 600 °C, the V and Mo contents are 60.19% and 33.66%, respectively. These values change to 45.05% and 43.92% at 620 °C and to 40.20% and 46.31% at 650 °C, respectively. As the annealing temperature increases from 600 to 650 °C, the Mo content in the VC precipitates progressively increases, which may be attributed to the enhanced thermal stability of MC-type carbides provided by Mo. As shown in  Fig. 10 
                         , the Thermo-Calc calculations indicate that the VC phase is not completely dissolved at 900 °C. The residual VC particles may undergo further coarsening during austenitization and subsequent intercritical annealing. This process reduces the total precipitate-matrix interfacial area and, through minimization of the interfacial energy, promotes the formation of relatively coarse and compact ellipsoidal or disc-like particles. Accordingly, the coarse ellipsoidal and disc-like precipitates observed after intercritical annealing at 600-650 °C are likely associated with the retention and subsequent coarsening of undissolved VC particles.

Fig. 11 
                          shows the statistical results of VC precipitates in the experimental steel after annealing at different temperatures. The average sizes of VC particles after annealing at 600 °C, 620 °C, and 650 °C are 9.1 nm, 10.2 nm, and 12.9 nm, respectively ( Fig. 11 (a)), while their number densities are 2.0 × 10 14  m −2 , 4.5 × 10 14  m −2 , and 5.4 × 10 14  m −2 , respectively ( Fig. 11 (b)). Both the particle size and number density of VC precipitates increase with increasing annealing temperature. Previous studies have demonstrated that precipitates with sizes of 1-10 nm provide the most effective precipitation strengthening [ 15 ]. After annealing at 600, 620, and 650 °C, the fractions of VC particles with sizes of 1-10 nm are approximately 71%, 60%, and 51%, respectively, while the corresponding number densities of VC particles within this size range are approximately 1.4 × 10 14 , 2.7 × 10 14  and 2.8 × 10 14  m −2 , respectively.

When the annealing temperature increases from 600 °C to 620 °C, although the fraction of fine VC particles decreases by about 10%, their number density nearly doubles (an increase of ∼93%). However, when the annealing temperature is further increased from 620 °C to 650 °C, the fraction of fine VC particles decreases by around 9%, while the number density increases only slightly (∼3%). These results indicate that at 600-620 °C, the precipitation of fine VC particles becomes more complete with increasing temperature. Although a portion of the VC particles begins to coarsen, the formation of fine VC precipitates remains dominant. In contrast, when the annealing temperature is in the range of 620-650 °C, VC particles become nearly fully precipitated, and further temperature increase leads predominantly to coarsening of the precipitates.

The HRTEM characterization of precipitates in the experimental steel after annealing at different temperatures is shown in  Fig. 12 
                         . For annealing temperatures of 600 °C and 620 °C, the characterized precipitates are VC particles newly precipitated during annealing, with sizes of approximately 10 nm ( Fig. 12 (a, b)). In contrast, the precipitates characterized at 650 °C are undissolved VC particles retained from quenching, with sizes of around 45 nm ( Fig. 12 (c)). Fourier transformation of the HRTEM images was performed using the Digital Micrograph software to obtain the diffraction patterns of the regions marked by red rectangles. Subsequently, inverse Fourier transformation was applied to specific lattice planes to reveal their lattice arrangements, and the interplanar spacings were measured. For the HRTEM image of the specimen annealed at 600 °C, the Fourier-transformed diffraction pattern corresponds to an FCC structure, as shown in  Fig. 12 (a). The measured interplanar spacing of the (002) plane is 0.2170 nm ( Fig. 12 (d)). The interplanar spacing of an FCC crystal can be calculated by the following equation:

The lattice constant of VC is typically taken as 0.4182 nm. Substituting this value into Eq.  (3)  yields a theoretical interplanar spacing of 0.2091 nm for the (002) plane of VC. The experimentally measured spacing is larger than the theoretical value, indicating that additional alloying elements such as Mn, Mo, and Si are dissolved in the VC particles during annealing, resulting in lattice distortion and an increase in the interplanar spacing [ 40 ]. Similarly, Fourier and inverse Fourier transformations applied to the HRTEM images of specimens annealed at 620 °C and 650 °C show that the (111) interplanar spacings are 0.246 nm and 0.247 nm, respectively ( Fig. 12 (e, f)), both slightly larger than the theoretical spacing of 0.2414 nm for the (111) plane of VC. These results further suggest that the undissolved VC particles after annealing also contain dissolved alloying elements.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The strength variation of the experimental steel after annealing at different temperatures is shown in  Fig. 13 
                         . With increasing annealing temperature, both the tensile strength and yield strength decrease gradually. According to the previous results, the evolution trends of grain refinement strengthening ( Fig. 4 (d)) and precipitation strengthening ( Fig. 9 (a-c)) do not match the change in strength. In addition, the solid-solution strengthening effect should continuously increase at higher annealing temperatures [ 12 ]. Therefore, the change in strength is considered to be mainly dominated by the following two factors: first, the increased volume fraction of reverted austenite raises the proportion of the soft phase, thereby reducing strength; second, dislocation annihilation is promoted at higher annealing temperatures, leading to reduced dislocation strengthening. However, the reduction in tensile strength is smaller than that in yield strength with increasing annealing temperature. This is because the TRIP effect of reverted austenite provides additional strain hardening during deformation, partially compensating for the loss in strength [ 12 ]. Additionally,  Fig. 13 (b) shows that the elongation of the steel increases progressively with annealing temperature, which is consistent with the evolution of reverted austenite content ( Fig. 5 (b)). This is attributed to the TRIP effect of reverted austenite, which delays the onset of necking and thus enhances ductility [ 25 ].

Fig. 13 (a) shows the engineering stress-strain curves of the experimental steel after annealing at different temperatures. It can be observed that, after annealing at 650 °C, the curve exhibits non-periodic serrations, a phenomenon known as Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect, which indicates plastic instability during tensile deformation. Callahan et al. [ 41 ], using digital image correlation (DIC) and in situ magnetic-flux measurements, observed that strain-induced martensitic transformation occurred concurrently with propagating PLC bands. Sun et al. [ 42 ] further combined in situ magnetic measurements, XRD, and DIC and showed that localized austenite-to-martensite transformation occurred when a PLC band passed through the monitored region. These studies suggest that the PLC effect observed during room-temperature tensile deformation of medium-Mn steels is closely associated with the TRIP effect of retained austenite. In the present study, the specimen annealed at 650 °C exhibits the most pronounced serrated flow in its true stress–true strain curve, indicating more intense strain-induced transformation activity. The XRD results and DICTRA simulations show that this specimen contains the highest fraction of reverted austenite, while the simulations predict the lowest austenite stability. These results suggest that the pronounced TRIP effect during tensile deformation contributes substantially to the severe PLC behavior observed in the specimen annealed at 650 °C.

Fig. 14 
                          shows the work-hardening rate-true strain curves of the experimental steel after annealing at different temperatures. For the specimens annealed at 600 °C and 620 °C, the curves can be divided into three characteristic stages. Stage I corresponds to the early stage of deformation, during which the deformation mode transitions from elastic to plastic, and the matrix begins to yield, resulting in a nearly linear decrease in the work-hardening rate. Stage II is characterized by a slight increase in the work-hardening rate followed by gradual stabilization or a slow decline. At the beginning of this stage, the least stable reverted austenite undergoes TRIP transformation first, leading to a slight increase in the work-hardening rate. Subsequently, the more stable reverted austenite continues to transform progressively under stress, promoting sustained martensitic transformation, effectively delaying the onset of necking and causing the work-hardening rate to level off or slowly decrease. Stage III begins with the onset of necking and ends with fracture of the specimen, during which the work-hardening rate drops sharply. In this stage, a large portion of reverted austenite has transformed, weakening the TRIP effect. The strengthening contributions from martensitic transformation and dislocation multiplication during deformation are no longer sufficient to maintain the work-hardening level, resulting in a rapid decline until fracture. For the specimen annealed at 650 °C, the work-hardening-rate curve can likewise be divided into three stages, with Stages I and III exhibiting trends similar to those described above, although the overall work-hardening rate remains relatively high. Stage II, however, is characterized by pronounced serrated fluctuations associated with the PLC effect.

Fig. 15 
                         (a) shows the impact absorbed energy at 0 °C for the experimental steel after annealing at different temperatures. As the annealing temperature increases, the impact energy continuously decreases, which is in stark contrast to the variation trends of reverted austenite content and elongation with annealing temperature. As discussed in Section 3.2, increasing the annealing temperature leads to an increase in the size of reverted austenite and a reduction in the average C and Mn concentrations within austenite, thereby decreasing its stability. Therefore, when the fraction of reverted austenite reaches a certain level, its stability becomes the dominant factor influencing the impact toughness of the steel. This observation is consistent with the findings reported by Huang [ 43 ]. The SEM images of the impact fracture surfaces after annealing at different temperatures are shown in  Fig. 15 (b–d). Regardless of the annealing temperature, the impact fracture surfaces exhibit a mixed fracture mode of dimples and quasi-cleavage features. Compared with other annealing conditions, the specimen annealed at 600 °C exhibits the largest dimple size. With increasing annealing temperature, the proportion of large dimples decreases, resulting in a gradual reduction in impact energy [ 44 ]. The evolution of fracture morphology is therefore consistent with the change in impact toughness.

The analysis of precipitates in Section 3.3 indicates that the finely and homogeneously dispersed precipitates are mainly VC ( Fig. 9 ). Given the relatively long annealing time and the comparatively low annealing temperatures, it can be assumed that VC precipitates completely within the ferrite matrix, and thus the precipitation strengthening contribution in austenite can be neglected. The theoretical strengthening increments and calculated yield strength ( σ 
                         y-calc ), along with the experimentally measured yield strength ( σ 
                         y-exp ) after annealing at different temperatures, are summarized in  Table 2 
                         . The calculated values are in good agreement with the experimental results, indicating that the strengthening model effectively reflects the influence of annealing temperature on the strengthening behavior. When annealed at 650 °C, the reverted austenite contributes only ∼170 MPa to the strengthening increment, and thus the strengthening effects of ferrite remain the dominant contributors to the yield strength.

For all annealing conditions, grain boundary strengthening and dislocation strengthening are the primary strengthening mechanisms in the ferritic matrix. With increasing annealing temperature, the grain boundary strengthening and precipitation strengthening increments slightly increase, while the solid-solution strengthening remains nearly unchanged. These trends are consistent with the microstructural observations ( Figs. 4 and 10 ). Among the various strengthening mechanisms, dislocation strengthening is most significantly affected by annealing temperature. As the temperature increases from 600 °C to 620 °C, the dislocation strengthening increment decreases markedly by approximately 301 MPa. With a further temperature increase to 650 °C, it decreases by an additional ∼47 MPa. Therefore, the pronounced reduction in dislocation strengthening is the primary reason for the decrease in yield strength when the annealing temperature increases from 600 °C to 620 °C. When the temperature further rises to 650 °C, besides the continued reduction of dislocation strengthening, the higher content of the soft reverted austenite phase also contributes to the decrease in yield strength.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
1. 
                            As the annealing temperature increases from 600 °C to 650 °C, both the volume fraction and size of reverted austenite gradually increase. The increased fractions of reverted austenite and deformation-induced fresh martensite contribute to a reduction in the effective grain size. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            Thermo-Calc and DICTRA simulations indicate that increasing the annealing temperature results in coarsening of reverted austenite and decreasing average C and Mn concentrations within the austenite, leading to a reduction in its chemical stability. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            Two types of precipitates are observed under different annealing temperatures: undissolved particles and newly formed precipitates, both primarily composed of VC. With increasing annealing temperature, the amount of VC precipitates increases, while the coarsening of undissolved particles limits the further increase in precipitation strengthening. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            As the annealing temperature increases from 600 °C to 650 °C, the tensile strength, yield strength, and impact toughness decrease progressively, whereas the elongation continuously improves. These trends are mainly governed by the evolution of reverted austenite content and stability. After annealing at 600 °C, the steel exhibits an excellent strength-toughness balance, with a tensile strength of 1251 MPa, yield strength of 1193 MPa, and impact energy of 78 J at 0 °C. 
                         
                         
                            5. 
                            The work-hardening-rate curves exhibit similar overall trends at different annealing temperatures. However, the specimen annealed at 650 °C shows pronounced serrations in Stage II owing to the PLC effect and exhibits the highest work-hardening rate, which is attributed to its higher reverted-austenite fraction and the consequently enhanced TRIP effect. 
                         
                         
                            6. 
                            Theoretical calculations show that as the annealing temperature increases from 600 °C to 620 °C and 650 °C, the dislocation strengthening increment decreases significantly, from 577 MPa to 276 MPa and 229 MPa, respectively. The pronounced reduction in dislocation strengthening is the primary cause of yield strength degradation at 620 °C, while at 650 °C both the reduced dislocation strengthening and increased soft-phase reverted austenite contribute to the further decline in yield strength.
